title: The Akal Takht rebuilt
hook: Sikhs pulled down the government-repaired Akal Takht and rebuilt it by volunteer labor

segments.voice: Yesterday, peace returns, and your line was healing, slowly. A new week opens with a building that had to be torn down before it could heal.

A new building stands where a broken one stood. The walls are straight, the paint is fresh, the dome is whole. And the people it was built for won't accept it. They gather with hammers and baskets and take it apart, brick by brick, by hand. Then they start again, from the ground, carrying the new bricks themselves. It sounds like waste. To the Sikhs who did it at the Akal Takht, after June, it was the only way the building could be theirs again. The way they did it is today's word: kar seva.
screen: `A NEW BUILDING, REFUSED.` → `TAKEN APART BY HAND.` → `KAR SEVA.`

segments.voice: First, the throne. The Akal Takht, the throne of the Timeless One, stands facing the Darbar Sahib in Amritsar, the seat from which Sikh decisions and edicts go out. This path has met it before. In June it was badly damaged in the fighting. Second, the repair. The government had it repaired quickly, with a Nihang leader, Baba Santa Singh, at the head of the work. But to the Sikh bodies that speak for the panth, a throne repaired by the government that had broken it was not a throne. They called it the government's building, and the Akal Takht later censured Santa Singh for his part in it. Third, the rebuilding. Kar seva volunteers pulled the repaired building down and rebuilt the Akal Takht. Kar means work; seva means selfless service. Led by kar seva teams, volunteers carried earth, bricks and mortar on their heads, the way kar seva is done. No wage. No contract. Just hands. Fourth, the root. At Ang 286 of the Guru Granth Sahib, in the Sukhmani, Guru Arjan says that the one who serves without wanting anything in return reaches the Lord. In Sikh teaching, seva is not a side activity. It is a way the hands pray. And for a throne that stands for the panth's own voice, only the panth's own hands would do.
screen: `THE THRONE OF THE TIMELESS ONE.` · `REPAIRED BY THE GOVERNMENT, REFUSED.` · `PULLED DOWN, REBUILT BY HAND.` · `ANG 286: SERVE, WANTING NOTHING.` · then, large: `BUILT BY VOLUNTEERS.`

segments.voice: Picture where an hour of your hands could help: a food bank, a cleanup, a gurdwara kitchen, a neighbor's garden, a shelter. Breathe in and see yourself arriving; breathe out and see the work, carrying, washing, sweeping, stirring, with no one paying you and no one thanking you. If you pray, let Waheguru go with the picture.
Kar seva. Kar is work, seva is selfless service: volunteer labor that builds and cleans the Gurus' places, and that rebuilt the Akal Takht. Today's word.
Your line: built by volunteers. Just hands, the panth's own, carrying the bricks. A new week begins.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember the rebuilding of the Akal Takht by kar seva as a statement that the panth's throne must be built by the panth itself; kar seva volunteers still build and clean gurdwaras by hand.

notes: New week starts here (days 1016–1022). No dates are given on purpose (claims rule): neither the repair, the demolition nor the completion of the rebuilt Akal Takht is dated.

'This path has met it many times' refers to earlier days on the Akal Takht; confirm.
'as Sikhs have done at shrines for generations' is a general claim; tomorrow's day (Building by hand) covers kar seva broadly, so today keeps to the Akal Takht.
